title: Learning Lesson 2: Attention is Narrow
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This lesson opens Chew's four-bottleneck framework by introducing the first and most fundamental limitation: attention is narrow. Stuart uses a parking-lot traffic analogy to define what a cognitive "bottleneck" or "choke point" means before naming all four bottlenecks the series will cover. He then makes the narrowness of attention experientially vivid by walking students through everything competing for their focus in a single classroom moment — sights, sounds, pockets, plans for the weekend — before landing on the flashlight-in-a-dark-room metaphor: attention illuminates only a small circle at a time, no matter how much is actually in the room. The prescribed solution is simple but, as Stuart notes, easy to ignore: eliminate distractions, applied strategically rather than permanently (not removing siblings from your life, but minimizing them as a distraction while learning). He closes with a real student example — physically removing a phone from the room while studying — as a model of what proactively managing this bottleneck looks like in practice.
points: Stuart defines a learning "bottleneck" using a school-parking-lot traffic analogy before introducing Chew's four bottlenecks, making an abstract cognitive-science term concrete for teenagers.

The flashlight-in-a-dark-room metaphor captures the core claim of the lesson: attention only illuminates a small portion of everything available to notice at any moment, regardless of how much there is to attend to.
The prescribed solution, eliminate distractions, is deliberately framed as "boringly obvious" specifically because Stuart's point is that obvious solutions are the ones people most often skip.

A real student example — physically removing her phone from the room while studying, rather than just silencing it — models proactive, structural distraction elimination rather than relying on willpower.
quotes: Have you ever seen what happens at the end of every school day in the student parking lot? Cars start lining up, right? Because those exits are bottlenecks. They are what Dr. Chew would call "choke points.

So there are a LOT of things that you can think about just sitting right here in my world history class, aren't there? A LOT. But the trouble is, you can't think about all of those things at the same time, can you?
And part of that is because attention is narrow. It's like a flashlight beam in a pitch dark room. Will the whole room be illuminated? No. Just a circle, right?
Wow, right? Eliminate distractions. How boringly obvious is that!? But here's a secret: it's the obvious stuff that people most often ignore.

She'd turn her phone off, and then she'd put it outside her bedroom door, and then she'd close her door. This way, she said, she didn't have to even see her phone — didn't even have to have it in the same room.
